column2:
Your retail analytics team is moving a service from the Claude API to Claude on Vertex AI. The service builds Messages API requests by hand with an HTTP client. After pointing it at the Vertex rawPredict endpoint, every request is rejected with a validation error, even though the messages, max_tokens, and tools fields are unchanged.

Which TWO changes to the request are required for Vertex AI? (Select TWO.)

A. Prefix the model name with publishers/anthropic/ inside the model field of the body.
B. Send anthropic-version: vertex-2023-10-16 as an HTTP header in place of the Claude API header value.
C. Add anthropic_version to the JSON body with the value vertex-2023-10-16.
D. Remove model from the JSON body and specify the model in the endpoint URL path instead.
column3:
Correct Answer: C and D. Options C and D are the two documented differences between the Claude API and Claude on Vertex AI: the model is part of the Google Cloud endpoint URL (.../publishers/anthropic/models/<model>:rawPredict) rather than the body, and anthropic_version is passed in the body with the fixed value vertex-2023-10-16 rather than as a header; everything else in the Messages API body is the same. Option B keeps the version in a header; on Vertex the version is read from the anthropic_version body field, so a header does not satisfy the requirement whatever value it carries. Option A keeps the model in the body, which Vertex does not accept; the publisher path belongs in the URL. Currency note (Oct 2026): Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and Anthropic's docs title this page Claude on Google Cloud, but the endpoint path, rawPredict and the vertex-2023-10-16 value are unchanged.

column2:
A logistics team's Vertex AI integration works with claude-haiku-4-5@20251001. A developer copies a model string from a Claude API example, claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, into the same AnthropicVertex client, and every request now fails with a not-found error, although the model is enabled in Model Garden.

What is the cause?

A. The Vertex publisher model ID needs an anthropic. prefix in front of the Claude model name.
B. The model name has to be repeated in the anthropic_version field of the request body.
C. Vertex serves Claude models under undated alias names such as claude-haiku-4-5 and rejects dated versions.
D. The Vertex model ID joins the snapshot date to the name with @, not the hyphen used in the Claude API form.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: for Claude models whose ID carries a snapshot date, the Vertex AI publisher model ID separates the date with @ (claude-haiku-4-5@20251001), while the Claude API ID uses a hyphen (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001), so the hyphenated string matches no publisher model in the endpoint path. Option A describes the Amazon Bedrock naming convention, not Vertex. Option B misuses anthropic_version, which carries the fixed API version string vertex-2023-10-16, never a model name. Option C contradicts the working integration, which addresses a dated version. Currency note (Oct 2026): from the Claude 4.6 generation on, model IDs are dateless and the same on both platforms (for example claude-sonnet-4-6), so this mismatch arises only with earlier dated models, and Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

Your media company's content pipeline runs on Cloud Run and must call Claude through Vertex AI in your Google Cloud project. A developer instantiates the standard anthropic.Anthropic() client, sets base_url to the Vertex AI endpoint, and passes the model in messages.create(). Requests fail because the body still carries model and lacks the Vertex API version field.

What is the correct way to use the Anthropic SDK here?

A. Install anthropic[vertex] and create AnthropicVertex(project_id=..., region=...), which targets the publisher endpoint for you.
B. Keep the Anthropic client, set base_url to the regional endpoint, and add anthropic_version through extra_body on every call.
C. Use the Google GenAI SDK's Gemini generate_content method with the Claude model ID as the model name.
D. Keep the Anthropic client and pass the Google Cloud project ID as the api_key so requests are attributed to the project.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: the SDK ships a Vertex-specific client, AnthropicVertex, installed through the anthropic[vertex] extra and constructed with your project_id and region; it places the model in the publisher endpoint URL, adds anthropic_version, and picks up your Google Cloud credentials, so messages.create() calls stay unchanged. Option B still sends model in the body and targets the wrong path. Option C is Gemini's request format, not the Messages API that Claude expects. Option D confuses a project ID with an API key; Vertex is not authenticated that way. Currency note (Oct 2026): Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and Anthropic's docs say Claude on Google Cloud, but the anthropic[vertex] extra and the AnthropicVertex class keep their names.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration)

References:

column2:
A retail analytics assistant on Vertex AI is pinned to a single region with region="us-east5". During peak hours about 4% of requests still fail with resource-exhausted errors after the client's retries with backoff, while other regions have capacity. The team has no data-residency requirement and does not use provisioned throughput.

What is the most appropriate change?

A. Raise max_retries on the client and resend each failed request to the same region up to five more times.
B. Create the client with region="global" and let requests route dynamically to regions with available capacity.
C. Switch to a smaller model such as claude-haiku-4-5@20251001 and draw less regional capacity on each request.
D. Create a second client with a different region value and alternate requests between the two regions.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: the global endpoint routes each request dynamically to a region with available capacity, which is exactly what maximizes availability when residency is flexible, and the SDK selects it when region is "global". Option A keeps resending to a region that is out of capacity, which the existing retries already show is not enough. Option C changes the model rather than the capacity problem and may reduce quality. Option D reimplements a crude version of what the global endpoint already does, with only two regions and extra client logic. Currency note (Oct 2026): Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and current docs add multi-region endpoints (us, eu) for teams that need residency within a geography.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration)

References:
• Claude on Google Cloud — Global, multi-region, and regional endpoints
• Partner models — Regional, global, and multi-region endpoints (Google Cloud docs)

column2:
You are standing up a new Google Cloud project for a logistics operations assistant. Gemini requests from the project succeed, but the first request to a Claude publisher model through AnthropicVertex is rejected with an error saying the model is not accessible to the project.

What is the most likely missing setup step?

A. Setting the client's region parameter to the same region in which the project's other Vertex resources were created.
B. Adding anthropic_version to the request body so that Vertex recognizes the publisher.
C. Enabling that Claude model in Vertex AI Model Garden, which must be done per model before it can be called.
D. Installing the google-genai package alongside the Anthropic SDK so the project can reach partner models.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Claude models are partner models in Model Garden; you search for Anthropic, open the model, and click Enable (if no Enable button appears, access already exists). Until that is done the project cannot call the model even though other Vertex services work. Option A: region affects availability, not project access. Option B: the SDK already sends anthropic_version, and it does not grant access. Option D: the Google GenAI SDK is not needed to call Claude through the Anthropic SDK. Currency note (Oct 2026): Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform; Model Garden keeps its name and the per-model Enable step is unchanged.

column2:
Your media company's pipeline calls Claude on Vertex AI with region="global" in development. For production, compliance asks that requests stay in one specific Google Cloud region. After switching the client to that region, calls to the same enabled model return not-found errors, while a different Claude model works there.

What best explains this, and what should you do?

A. Regional endpoints require the anthropic. model prefix; add the prefix to the model ID and keep the chosen region.
B. The model must be enabled again in each region; enable it from that region's Model Garden page and retry.
C. Regional endpoints serve only the newest model in each family; upgrade to the latest model ID and keep the region.
D. Model availability varies by region; check which regions offer this model and choose one that meets compliance.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: not every Claude model is offered in every region. The global endpoint hides this because it routes dynamically, but a regional endpoint only serves models available in that region, so you must choose a region that both offers the model and satisfies the residency requirement; Model Garden and Google's Claude model pages list the regions for each model. Option A applies a Bedrock convention. Option B is wrong: a model is enabled once, from its Model Garden model card, with no per-region step. Option C invents a rule; availability is listed per model and region, not granted to the newest model. Currency note (Oct 2026): Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and current docs say models newer than Claude Sonnet 4.6 are served only through the global or multi-region (us, eu) endpoints.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration)

column2:
A logistics operations assistant on Vertex AI must answer two kinds of questions: procedures from 900 internal standard-operating-procedure documents stored in Cloud Storage, and current carrier service alerts posted on public carrier websites. The team enabled the web search tool and found that SOP questions are answered incorrectly 70% of the time, while alert questions are accurate.

What is the right architecture?

A. Set allowed_domains to the company's intranet domain and keep answering both question types with web search.
B. Raise max_uses to let Claude run many more searches on each SOP question before it writes its answer.
C. Build a retrieval pipeline over the SOP documents and keep the web search tool for the public alert questions.
D. Put the Cloud Storage links to the SOPs in the system prompt and ask Claude to open them when it needs a procedure.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: web search is a server-side tool that queries the public web and cannot see private documents in your bucket, so no configuration of the tool will surface SOP content. Retrieval over your own documents (chunk, index, retrieve into the prompt) is the mechanism for private data, while web search remains the right tool for current public information. Option A restricts search to a domain the search engine cannot index. Option B spends more searches on an index that lacks the data. Option D: web search cannot open private bucket objects, and links in a prompt are not searchable content.

column2:
Your media company's fact-checking assistant uses the web search tool on Vertex AI. In a review of 200 answers, 35% cited content-farm blogs, while your editorial policy allows only 12 named news and reference publishers. The system prompt already says 'use only reputable sources'.

What is the most reliable fix?

A. Add an allowed_domains list with the 12 approved publisher domains to the web search tool definition.
B. Strengthen the system prompt with the 12 domain names and an instruction to ignore all other sites.
C. Add both an allowed_domains list of the 12 publishers and a blocked_domains list of known content farms.
D. Filter the returned citations client-side and drop any statement whose source is not on the approved list.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: allowed_domains is applied by the API to the searches it runs, so results come only from the listed domains before Claude reads any of them; entries are bare domains such as example.com, optionally with a path, and carry no scheme. Option B is prompt-only guidance that the 35% failure rate already shows to be insufficient. Option C is rejected by the API: a request may include allowed_domains or blocked_domains, not both, and a request with both returns a 400 error. Option D discards content after Claude has already reasoned over it, producing gaps in answers rather than better sourcing.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.5

References:
• Web search tool — Domain filtering
• Server tools — Domain filtering

column2:
A retail analytics team uses the web search tool on Vertex AI to check competitor prices. Traces show that 15% of requests perform 12 or more searches in a single turn, driving p95 latency to 40 seconds and most of the request cost, while answers stop improving after the third search. Each search already returns several results.

What change most directly bounds the work per request?

A. Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to run at most three searches for any single request it handles.
B. Set max_uses: 3 on the web search tool definition so further searches in that request are refused.
C. Lower max_tokens so that turns with many searches run out of output budget and are cut off sooner.
D. Set a 10-second client timeout and cancel any request that is still running when the timer expires.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: max_uses is enforced server-side. Once the limit is reached, further search attempts return a max_uses_exceeded error inside the tool result and Claude answers with what it has, so latency and cost are bounded deterministically. Option A is prompt-only and not guaranteed. Option C limits output tokens, not the number of searches, and would truncate answers. Option D discards partial work and returns nothing for the slowest requests instead of bounding them.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.5

References:
• Web search tool — Max uses
• Web search tool — Errors
• Web search with Anthropic Claude models (Google Cloud docs)

column2:
Your logistics assistant answers questions about carrier service disruptions using the web search tool on Vertex AI. Users say they cannot tell which statements come from real sources; the UI currently shows only the answer's text, joined into one plain paragraph. A spot check also found two URLs that Claude had typed into its answers and that lead to no page.

Which TWO changes give users verifiable sourcing? (Select TWO.)

A. Add a line to the system prompt asking Claude to end each answer with a plain-text list of the URLs it consulted.
B. Render each text block's citations entries (url, title, cited_text) next to the sentence they support.
C. List the sources from the web_search_tool_result block (title and URL of each web_search_result) alongside the answer.
D. Display the input query of each server_tool_use block beneath the answer as the sources behind it.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and C. Options B and C are correct. A web search response is a sequence of blocks: server_tool_use (the query), web_search_tool_result holding web_search_result entries with title and URL, and text blocks, some carrying citations with the source URL, title, and cited text; rendering the citations beside the statements they support and listing the retrieved sources is how the course recommends surfacing provenance. Option A relies on Claude writing out URLs in prose, which is unverifiable and can be wrong, as the spot check showed. Option D shows what Claude searched for, not what it found: a query string is not a source, and it ties no statement to a page the user can open.

column2:
Your retail analytics team is migrating an assistant with 11 custom tools from the Claude API to Claude on Vertex AI. A developer proposes rewriting every tool as a Gemini-style function declaration, arguing that Vertex has its own tool format; the rewrite would take about two weeks.

What should the team do?

A. Rewrite the tools as Gemini function declarations and route calls through Vertex's own function-calling layer.
B. Keep the existing tools definitions as they are and adapt the request envelope that Vertex expects around them.
C. Register each tool in Model Garden and let Vertex validate calls against the schemas before they reach the model.
D. Convert the schemas to OpenAPI documents and reference them from the system prompt instead of the tools parameter.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Claude on Vertex AI uses the Messages API format; the only differences are that the model is in the URL and anthropic_version is in the body, so the same JSON Schema tool definitions, tool_use blocks, and tool_result handling work unchanged. Option A adopts Gemini's format, which Claude publisher models do not use. Option C: Model Garden is where the model is enabled; tool definitions travel in each request's tools parameter. Option D moves the schemas out of the tools parameter, where Claude expects them. Currency note (Oct 2026): Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and Anthropic's docs title the page Claude on Google Cloud; the tool format is unchanged.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Claude on Google Cloud — Making requests
• Request predictions with Claude models — Tool use (function calling) (Google Cloud docs)
• Define tools — Specifying client tools

column2:
To cut request rounds, your logistics team adds a batch tool: a tool the team defines itself, whose invocations input is a list of tool names and arguments, so that Claude can ask for several tool calls in one tool_use block. In testing, Claude calls the batch tool, but the dispatcher that routes each tool call to its handler raises an unknown-tool error, and a colleague proposes deleting the individual tool schemas so that Claude has to use the batch tool.

Which TWO steps are needed for the batch tool to work? (Select TWO.)

A. Delete the individual tool schemas from tools and leave just the batch tool schema for Claude to route its calls through.
B. Keep the individual tool schemas in tools next to the batch tool schema and let Claude read their parameters.
C. Return a separate tool_result for each invocation in the list, each reusing the batch call's tool_use_id.
D. Add a handler branch that runs each invocation through the existing dispatcher and returns the combined output as one result.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and D. Options B and D are correct. The batch tool is an ordinary developer-defined tool: you supply its schema and its implementation, and it is an abstraction over the other tools, which stay in the tool list so Claude knows their parameters when it writes invocations. Its handler loops over the invocations, calls each named tool through the same dispatcher used for direct calls, and returns the combined outputs as the one result of the batch tool_use. Option A removes the schemas Claude needs to build invocations. Option C mismatches results to requests: the batch call is a single tool_use and expects exactly one tool_result. Currency note (Oct 2026): Claude 4 and later models make parallel tool calls by default, so current docs get several calls per turn without a batch tool; Anthropic's cookbook presents the pattern as a workaround for Claude 3.7 Sonnet.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3

References:
• Parallel tool calls on Claude 3.7 Sonnet — Introducing a batch tool (Claude Cookbook)
• Parallel tool use — Maximizing parallel tool use
• Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools

column2:
Your media company wants Claude to fix configuration files in a workspace mounted on a Cloud Run worker. The team adds the text editor tool stub (type and name only) to tools on Vertex AI. Claude responds with tool_use blocks such as view and str_replace, but no file ever changes and the loop stalls.

What is missing?

A. A full input_schema in the tool definition that lists each editor command together with the arguments it takes.
B. A larger max_tokens value in the request, sized for the longest edit command that Claude writes.
C. A handler in your code that runs each editor command on the workspace and returns the outcome as a tool_result.
D. The contents of the workspace files pasted into the system prompt before the conversation starts.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: only the text editor tool's schema is built into Claude, which is why the definition carries just type and name; the implementation is yours. Your code must handle view, create, str_replace, and the other commands against the file system and return each outcome in a tool_result, just as with any custom tool. Option A duplicates a schema Claude already has; the built-in schema cannot be supplied or modified. Option B: the commands are complete; nothing acts on them. Option D misunderstands the tool, which reads files through your view handler.

References:
• Text editor tool — Implement the text editor tool
• How tool use works — Anthropic-schema tools (client-executed)
• Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools

column2:
A logistics team's file-editing agent on Vertex AI has run for months with a text editor tool stub whose type string carries a date. After upgrading to a newer Claude model version, every request fails with an error that the tool type is not supported by the model, before any edit is attempted.

What is the correct fix?

A. Add an explicit input_schema to the stub so that the model can validate the tool definition.
B. Remove the name field, since newer models infer it from the type string.
C. Downgrade the anthropic_version body field to match the older tool definition.
D. Update the stub's type string to the text editor version that corresponds to the new model.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: the type string in a text editor tool definition names a dated tool version, and which version a model accepts depends on the model: text_editor_20250728 is for Claude 4 and later models and text_editor_20250124 is for earlier ones. Each version also fixes the tool's name, so check that when the type changes. Option A: the schema is built into the model and cannot be supplied or modified. Option B: the name is required. Option C: anthropic_version is the fixed Vertex API version and is unrelated to tool versions.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Tool reference — Tool versioning
• Text editor tool — Change log
• Claude on Google Cloud — Making requests

column2:
Your retail assistant's tool loop on Vertex AI sends tools on the first request only. When Claude requests lookup_inventory, your code runs it, appends the assistant turn and a tool_result message, and calls the API again without tools. In code review, a colleague says that second call is built incorrectly.

What is the fix?

A. Include the same tools list on every request in the loop, including the ones that return tool results.
B. Remove the tool_use and tool_result blocks from history and resend the tool output as plain text in a user message.
C. Send the tool result in an assistant message instead of a user message on the follow-up call.
D. Start a fresh conversation for the follow-up request and include only the tool output in its first message.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: once tools are introduced, every request in the conversation must carry the tool definitions, including follow-up requests that deliver tool_result blocks, because the tool_use and tool_result blocks in the history refer to those tools, and Claude may need to call one again. Option B destroys the structured pairing Claude uses to relate results to requests. Option C: tool results are sent in a user message. Option D discards the conversation context that the tool call was serving.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3

References:
• Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools
• How tool use works — The agentic loop (client tools)
• Troubleshooting tool use — Errors at request time

column2:
Your logistics assistant on Vertex AI combines three custom tools with the web search tool. The tool loop treats every non-text block as a tool request: when a response contains a server_tool_use block for web_search, the handler looks it up in the dispatcher, fails, and sends back an error tool_result for it, and the next request fails validation.

How should the loop handle these blocks?

A. Add a web_search entry to the dispatcher that calls a third-party search API and returns its results in a tool_result block.
B. Strip server_tool_use blocks from the assistant message before storing it in the conversation history.
C. Send the web search tool and the custom tools in separate requests and merge the answers in application code.
D. Run tool_use blocks through the dispatcher and leave server_tool_use blocks to the platform without a tool_result.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: web search is a server tool. The platform runs the search and returns the outcome in a web_search_tool_result block, so the client loop must never execute or answer a server_tool_use block; only tool_use blocks for your custom tools require a tool_result. If the same turn also calls one of your tools, the search result can arrive in a later response, after you return only the client tool_result blocks. Option A duplicates a search the platform performs and sends a result for an ID that expects none. Option B alters assistant content that must be passed back unchanged in later turns. Option C is unnecessary: server and client tools can coexist in one request, and a web-search-only request would still return server_tool_use blocks that the loop must not answer.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3

References:
• Server tools — The server_tool_use block
• Server tools — Mixing server tools and client tools in one turn
• Handle tool calls — Handling results from server tools

column2:
A logistics team wants Claude to apply small changes to 3,000-line YAML routing configurations from a Cloud Run job. The current design asks Claude to output the entire rewritten file, which costs about 40,000 output tokens per change and has introduced unrelated line drift in 8% of edits.

Which approach best fits this task?

A. Keep full-file rewrites but add a diff check that rejects output that changes lines outside the intended edit.
B. Split each file into 500-line pieces, rewrite just the piece that contains the change, and size max_tokens for one piece.
C. Provide the text editor tool and a handler, and have Claude apply str_replace edits to just the affected lines.
D. Turn on extended thinking with the thinking parameter and have Claude reproduce the untouched lines carefully.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: the text editor tool exists for programmatic file manipulation. Claude inspects the file with view and changes only the relevant text with str_replace, so output tokens scale with the edit rather than the file and untouched lines are never regenerated. Option A detects drift only after paying for the full rewrite. Option B still regenerates hundreds of lines per change and adds bookkeeping. Option D spends more tokens hoping a generative rewrite becomes exact, which no reasoning budget guarantees.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Text editor tool — When to use the text editor tool
• Text editor tool — str_replace
• Building effective agents — Appendix 2: Prompt engineering your tools (Anthropic engineering)

column2:
Your retail analytics team scores product listings with a parallelization workflow on Vertex AI: six focused calls (title, images, pricing, compliance, description, shipping) run at once and an aggregator call produces the final score. After a prompt edit, the compliance dimension's accuracy fell from 94% to 81%, while the other dimensions were unchanged.

What is the most efficient way to diagnose and fix the regression?

A. Re-run the full end-to-end eval on the aggregated scores after each candidate change to the aggregator prompt.
B. Evaluate the compliance subtask prompt alone against its own labeled cases and iterate on just that prompt.
C. Merge the six prompts back into a single call so that there is only one prompt to test and maintain after each edit.
D. Add extended thinking to all six subtask calls so that accuracy recovers across every dimension at once.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: a key benefit of parallelization is that each subtask has its own prompt that can be evaluated and improved independently, so the regression can be isolated to the compliance prompt and fixed without touching the others. Option A tests the wrong component and mixes the signal with aggregation. Option C gives up the focus and independent testability that motivated the design. Option D adds cost and latency to five healthy dimensions to fix one.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.2

References:
• Building effective agents — Workflow: Parallelization (Anthropic engineering)
• Define success criteria and build evaluations — Build evaluations

column2:
A media company's pipeline on Vertex AI must, for each topic: pick the most promising angle from trending data, research that angle, and then write a 60-second script from the research. A developer proposes running the three Claude calls in parallel to cut latency from 24 seconds to about 9.

Why will this not work, and what structure fits?

A. The steps depend on each other's output, so they must be chained in order; parallelization suits independent subtasks.
B. Parallel calls share one conversation, so the three prompts would interfere; use separate system prompts instead.
C. Three calls exceed the parallel limit for a single request; batch them into a single tool call instead.
D. The steps are dependent, so a single combined prompt that does all three is the only way to preserve their ordering.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: parallelization splits a task into subtasks that can run simultaneously because they are independent. Here research needs the chosen angle and the script needs the research, so the work is a chain in which each call feeds the next. Option B misdescribes parallel calls, which are separate requests. Option C invents a limit. Option D is wrong that one combined prompt is the only way to keep the order: a chain keeps it too, and lets you inspect each step's output before the next call.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.2

References:
• Building effective agents — Workflow: Prompt chaining (Anthropic engineering)
• Building effective agents — Workflow: Parallelization (Anthropic engineering)
• Prompting best practices — Chain complex prompts

column2:
Your logistics team currently checks each shipment exception with a sequential chain of five focused Claude calls on Vertex AI, averaging 2 seconds each. Finance asks whether converting the chain into a five-way parallel fan-out with an aggregator call will lower monthly spend.

What should you tell them?

A. Latency falls to about one call plus the aggregator, and cost falls by about half because the parallel calls share one processed context.
B. Latency stays about the same, and cost falls by about a third because the aggregator call replaces some of the separate calls.
C. Latency falls to about one call plus the aggregator, and cost stays similar or rises slightly because of the extra aggregator call.
D. Latency and cost both stay about the same because fan-out mainly improves accuracy through prompts focused on one subtask.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: fan-out runs the five subtasks simultaneously, so wall-clock time approaches the slowest single call plus the aggregator, but every subtask is still a separate billed call and the aggregator adds one more, so token cost is similar to the chain or slightly higher. Option A gets the latency right but not the cost: parallel requests do not share processing, so each call is billed for its own tokens. Option B gets both wrong: the aggregator consumes the subtask outputs rather than replacing any of the calls, and running the calls in parallel does cut wall-clock time. Option D gets the cost right but ignores the latency gain, which is the main reason to fan out.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6

Your logistics assistant on Vertex AI uses a routing workflow: a classification call assigns each request to one of six pipelines, each with its own prompt and tools. After a change, the end-to-end eval fell from 91% to 78%, with failures spread across several pipelines whose prompts were not modified.

Where should you look first?

A. Evaluate the routing call by itself on labeled requests, since one misroute sends a request down the wrong pipeline.
B. Add extended thinking to all six pipeline prompts to make each of them more robust to unusual or ambiguous inputs.
C. Have the router emit a confidence score and send its low-confidence requests to a larger, more capable model instead.
D. Merge the six pipelines into one general prompt with every tool so that a routing error can no longer occur at all.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: in a routing workflow a single classification decides the entire downstream path, so a router regression shows up as failures scattered across otherwise unchanged pipelines, and because the steps are known the router can be evaluated in isolation against labeled inputs. Option B treats symptoms in components that did not change. Option C relies on self-reported confidence, which is not a reliable signal, and adds cost without finding the fault. Option D discards the specialization that routing provides.

column2:
Your logistics routing workflow classifies requests into six categories, each with a specialized prompt and tool set. In the last month, 9% of requests concern customs paperwork, which fits none of the categories; the router assigns them to 'tracking', whose pipeline lacks the tools to help, and users receive irrelevant answers.

What is the right change?

A. Give every pipeline access to all tools so that any misrouted request can still be completed.
B. Instruct the tracking pipeline to detect customs questions and answer them from general knowledge.
C. Have the router return two candidate categories and run both pipelines, keeping the better answer.
D. Add a 'customs' category to the router and build a pipeline with a prompt and tools specialized for it.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: routing works by mapping inputs to predefined categories with a dedicated downstream pipeline for each, so a recurring request type with no category is a gap in the category set, and the fix is to add the category and its specialized pipeline. Option A undoes the separation of tools that makes each pipeline reliable. Option B stretches a pipeline beyond its purpose without the needed tools. Option C doubles cost and latency for every request to paper over a missing route.

• Building effective agents — Workflow: Routing (Anthropic engineering)

column2:
Your logistics operations agent on Vertex AI plans its own tool calls for every request and completes 88% of them. Log analysis shows that three request types (reschedule delivery, update address, resend label) make up 80% of traffic and always require the same three tool calls in the same order.

What change most improves reliability?

A. Cap the agent at eight tool calls per request and return an error to the user whenever that cap is reached.
B. Move to a larger model with extended thinking so that the agent plans the three common requests more reliably.
C. Implement the three common request types as fixed workflows and keep the agent for the long tail.
D. Add more specialized tools so that the agent has one dedicated tool for each of the three common request types.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: when the exact steps are known in advance, a workflow is more accurate, easier to test, and more reliable than an agent; the course's recommendation is to prefer workflows wherever possible and reserve agents for genuinely open-ended requests. Option A uses an iteration cap as a control, which does not make the common paths succeed. Option B raises cost for a planning problem that does not need planning. Option D adds specialized tools, contrary to keeping agent tools general, and still depends on the agent's planning.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6

References:
• Building effective agents — When (and when not) to use agents (Anthropic engineering)
• Building effective agents — Agents (Anthropic engineering)

column2:
A media company's video agent on Vertex AI generates short clips with a bash tool that runs FFmpeg on a Compute Engine worker. FFmpeg exits with code 0 on every run, yet 15% of published clips have narration that starts several seconds after the point its script calls for, a point that differs for every clip, and the agent reports success each time.

Which change best lets the agent catch these defects before publishing?

A. Instruct the agent to inspect each render with its bash tool, pulling frames and timestamped captions to check timing.
B. Build a dedicated verify_video tool that returns pass or fail from a fixed heuristic applied to the clip's audio waveform.
C. Ask the agent to report a confidence score after each render and re-render the clip whenever the score falls below 0.8.
D. Re-render every clip twice and always publish the second one, since the first attempt is the one most prone to errors.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: a tool's return value (exit code 0) says the command ran, not that the result is right, so the agent needs a way to inspect its environment after acting. The course's approach is to guide the agent, through the system prompt, to use its general tools to examine the artifact, such as extracting screenshots with FFmpeg and caption timestamps with Whisper, so it can judge the result against the script and redo the work. Option B hard-codes one heuristic, but the right narration start differs for every clip. Option C relies on self-reported confidence. Option D re-renders without any check of the result.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6

References:
• Building effective agents — Agents (Anthropic engineering)
• Bash tool

column2:
Your retail returns agent on Vertex AI has get_current_datetime, add_duration, and lookup_order tools. When a customer asks 'when does my 30-day return window close?' without an order number, the agent assumes the purchase was today in 40% of cases and states a wrong date.

What design change best addresses this?

A. Default the purchase date to today inside add_duration whenever the caller leaves the date argument out.
B. Let the agent ask the customer for the order number or purchase date and relay that question as the turn's response.
C. Add a pre-parser that extracts dates from the message before Claude is called and rejects messages that lack one.
D. Limit the agent to two tool calls per request and return whatever result it has reached when the limit is hit.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: an agent can recognize that a tool call needs information it does not have and ask the user for it, and designing the loop so that a clarifying question is a valid turn outcome removes the incentive to guess. Option A bakes the wrong assumption into the tool. Option C is a brittle pre-parser that rejects legitimate requests instead of asking. Option D limits tool calls without addressing the missing input.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6

References:
• Building effective agents — Agents (Anthropic engineering)
• Tool use with Claude — When Claude uses tools

column2:
A retail analytics team is building semantic search over 50,000 product descriptions on Vertex AI. Their pipeline asks Claude Sonnet in a prompt to 'return a 768-dimensional embedding vector for this text' and stores the numbers it prints. Nearest-neighbor results are effectively random.

What should the pipeline use instead?

A. Claude with extended thinking enabled through the thinking parameter, prompted for vectors on both the chunks and each query.
B. Claude Opus (claude-opus-5-5) in place of Claude Sonnet, prompted for vectors on both the chunks and each query.
C. BM25 keyword matching in place of vector similarity, applied to both the indexed chunks and each query.
D. A dedicated Vertex AI embedding model such as text-embedding-005, applied to both the chunks and each query.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: Claude generates text, not embeddings, so a vector it writes out is just plausible-looking text. Vertex AI offers dedicated embedding models, accessed through the Google GenAI SDK, and the same model must embed both the stored chunks and each incoming query so their vectors are comparable. Options A and B still ask a text model to fabricate numbers. Option C gives up semantic matching entirely when a proper embedding model is available. Currency note (Oct 2026): Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform; its text embeddings page still lists text-embedding-005 and recommends gemini-embedding-001 for the highest quality.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4

References:
• Embeddings — How to get embeddings with Anthropic
• Get text embeddings — Supported models (Google Cloud docs)

column2:
Your logistics team's RAG pipeline over shipping SOPs uses size-based chunking with a chunk length of 150 characters and an overlap of 20. The top three retrieved chunks together hold under 450 characters, and in 60% of answers Claude says the context does not contain the procedure even when the correct chunk is among them.

What is the most appropriate first adjustment?

A. Retrieve the top 25 chunks instead of the top three so that more of the document reaches the prompt on every query.
B. Increase the chunk length to several hundred characters with overlap, so that each chunk carries a complete idea.
C. Switch to a model with a larger context window so that it can reason over the retrieved fragments more effectively.
D. Enable extended thinking so that Claude can reconstruct the full procedures from the fragments it is given.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: at 150 characters each chunk is a sentence fragment that cannot answer anything on its own; raising the size, with overlap, produces chunks that read as complete sections. Option A adds more fragments, but each is still an incomplete piece, and the neighbouring pieces of the procedure are not guaranteed to be retrieved or to arrive in order. Options C and D try to compensate for missing context with more model capacity, which cannot restore text that was never retrieved.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4

References:
• Contextual Retrieval — Implementation considerations (Anthropic engineering)
• Contextual Retrieval — A primer on RAG (Anthropic engineering)

column2:
A media company's knowledge base ingests its own markdown articles, which chunk cleanly on second-level headings, and now also accepts user-uploaded PDFs converted to plain text. For 30% of the PDFs, the header-based chunker returns a single chunk of 40,000 characters, and retrieval for those documents fails.

What is the right chunking design?

A. Keep header-based chunking for markdown and fall back to size-based chunking with overlap for unstructured documents.
B. Require users to convert PDFs to markdown with headings before upload and keep header-based chunking throughout.
C. Replace header-based chunking with semantic chunking by an NLP model across the whole knowledge base, markdown included.
D. Loosen the header pattern to treat a single # character as a chunk boundary in the converted PDF text.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: structure-based chunking depends on guarantees about the input format, and when those guarantees do not hold the course's guidance is to fall back to the reliable default, size-based chunking by character with overlap, while keeping the structural chunker for documents that qualify. Option B pushes the problem onto users and still fails for any unconverted file. Option C adds a complex technique when a simpler fallback resolves the failure. Option D changes a pattern that plain PDF text simply does not contain.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4

References:
• Contextual Retrieval — Implementation considerations (Anthropic engineering)
• Contextual Retrieval — A primer on RAG (Anthropic engineering)

column2:
Your retail search pipeline uses a retriever that forwards each query to a vector index and a BM25 index, both exposing add_document and search, and merges their ranked results. Product managers now want exact SKU matches (for example 'SKU-48213') to surface reliably, and an engineer proposes a regex pre-parser that bypasses the retriever for SKU-shaped queries.

Which design best fits the existing pipeline?

A. Add the regex pre-parser before the retriever and return the matching SKU record without calling either index's search.
B. Replace the BM25 index with a SKU lookup that exposes add_document and search in the BM25 index's place.
C. Implement SKU lookup as a third index with the same add_document and search interface and register it with the retriever.
D. Ask Claude in the answer prompt to recognize SKUs in the question and call the retriever's search as a tool.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: the multi-index retriever is designed for extension. Any search method that implements the shared interface can be added, and its results are merged with the others, so SKU lookups rank alongside semantic and lexical hits without special-casing queries. Option A introduces a brittle routing layer that skips the retriever and misses queries mixing a SKU with other text. Option B loses lexical matching for everything that is not a SKU. Option D moves retrieval into the generation step, adding latency and unreliability.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4

References:
• Contextual Retrieval — A primer on RAG (Anthropic engineering)
• Embeddings

column2:
Your retail analytics team enables extended thinking on Vertex AI with budget_tokens: 8000 for a demand-forecast explanation task and sets max_tokens: 8192. In production, 30% of responses contain a thinking block but the visible answer is empty or cut off after a sentence.

What is the cause and the fix?

A. The thinking budget is too small for the task; raise budget_tokens to 16000 while keeping max_tokens at 8192.
B. The model lacks a signal for when to end thinking; add a stop sequence so that it moves on to writing the answer sooner.
C. Extended thinking on Vertex AI requires streaming; enable streaming so that the whole answer is delivered in full.
D. Thinking tokens count toward max_tokens, leaving little for the answer; set max_tokens well above the budget.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: max_tokens bounds thinking and answer together, so it must exceed budget_tokens by a comfortable margin; with an 8,000 budget and an 8,192 cap, the answer can be at most 192 tokens whenever the model uses its full budget, which is why only some responses are cut off. Option A sets a budget larger than the cap, which the API rejects because budget_tokens must be less than max_tokens, and it targets the wrong quantity anyway. Option B: Claude ends its thinking on its own, and stop sequences apply to generated output text. Option C: streaming changes delivery, not the token budget. Currency note (Oct 2026): budget_tokens is deprecated on Claude 4.6 models and rejected by Claude 4.7 and later, which use adaptive thinking; thinking tokens still count toward max_tokens there.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output)

References:
• Extended thinking — Budget rules and tuning
• Troubleshooting thinking — The response stops with stop_reason: "max_tokens"

column2:
A logistics assistant on Vertex AI uses extended thinking with tools in multi-turn conversations. To save space, the app trims whitespace and truncates the thinking text of assistant turns to 500 characters before resending history. Since this change, requests that return tool results fail with a 400 error saying that thinking blocks cannot be modified.

What must the history code do?

A. Pass thinking and redacted_thinking blocks back exactly as received, signatures included, with no edits.
B. Recompute each block's signature locally over the truncated text with your own key before resending the history.
C. Convert earlier thinking blocks to ordinary text blocks so that no signature is checked on them when resent.
D. Increase budget_tokens so that the thinking text is short enough to keep intact.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: each thinking block carries a signature that the API uses to verify the block when it is sent back, and within a tool-use turn the assistant message must be returned exactly as received; edited, trimmed or truncated thinking is rejected. The same applies to redacted_thinking blocks, whose encrypted content must be returned unchanged. Option B is impossible; only the API can sign. Option C changes the block type and loses the reasoning context. Option D does not affect the integrity check. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs treat budget-based extended thinking as a legacy mode and newer models use adaptive thinking; the rule to return thinking blocks unmodified is the same.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output)

References:
• Thinking — Preserving thinking blocks
• Troubleshooting thinking — A 400 error says thinking blocks cannot be modified
• Thinking — Redacted thinking blocks

column2:
Your media company's pipeline on Vertex AI must extract figures and tables from 20-page PDF reports stored in Cloud Storage. A developer first passes the object's Cloud Storage URI as a document url source and then tries the Files API, and both are rejected on Vertex.

What is the correct way to provide the PDFs?

A. Convert each PDF to plain text with an OCR job first and send the text in a text content block.
B. Read the bytes from Cloud Storage and send them as a base64 document block with media type application/pdf.
C. Make the object publicly readable and pass its public web address in the url source of a document block.
D. Return the object's URI in a custom tool_result and let the model fetch the PDF itself after the call.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: PDF input is supported on Vertex AI, but URL sources and the Files API are not, so the supported path is to load the file bytes and send a document content block with base64 data and the application/pdf media type, the same shape as a base64 image block with the type and media type changed. Option A discards charts and tables that Claude can read directly. Option C is still a URL source, which Vertex does not accept, and it exposes the report. Option D: a URI in a tool result is only text; Claude cannot open the object, so the bytes would still have to be sent as base64. Currency note (Oct 2026): Google now calls Vertex AI the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and Anthropic's docs call the integration Claude on Google Cloud; the base64-only rule is unchanged.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output)

References:
• PDF support — Send your first PDF request
• Claude on Google Cloud — Features not supported

column2:
Your media company's research assistant on Vertex AI answers questions about 40-page PDF reports. Editors require every claim to link to the page it came from. The current pipeline extracts the PDF to plain text before the request, and the citations it gets back carry only character offsets, so the UI cannot show page numbers.

What change produces page-level citations?

A. Keep the text extraction and add a system instruction asking Claude to append the page number to each sentence it cites.
B. Insert 'Page N' markers after each 3,000 characters of extracted text and map each citation's start_char_index to its marker.
C. Send the original PDF as a document block with citations enabled and read the start and end page numbers from each citation.
D. Send each page of the PDF as an image block and read an image index from each citation in place of character offsets.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: the citation location type follows the source type. Plain-text documents yield character-location citations, while PDF documents yield page-location citations with start and end page numbers, plus the cited text and document title. Option A asks Claude to guess page numbers with no grounding. Option B approximates pages by character count, which breaks on tables and figures. Option D assumes citations can point at image indexes, but only text citations exist; images do not produce citations.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6

References:
• Citations — PDF documents
• Citations — Response structure
• Claude on Google Cloud — Supported feature highlights

column2:
Your logistics assistant on Vertex AI enables prompt caching with a breakpoint at the end of a 7,900-token system prompt. Usage data shows cache_creation_input_tokens of about 7,900 on every request and cache_read_input_tokens of 0, even for requests seconds apart. The system prompt begins with 'Current time:' and a timestamp, followed by the static instructions.

Why is the cache never read, and what fixes it?

A. Caching requires at least 8,192 tokens of content, so pad the system prompt with filler until it crosses that threshold.
B. The cached prefix must be identical across requests; move the timestamp to after the cache breakpoint.
C. Each request creates its own private cache; put the cache breakpoint on the user message instead of the system prompt.
D. The cache lifetime on Vertex AI is under a second; batch requests so that they all arrive at the same moment.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: a cache hit requires the content up to the breakpoint to be identical to the earlier request, and a per-request timestamp at the start of the system prompt changes the prefix every time, so every request writes a new cache and none reads one. Moving volatile content after the breakpoint keeps the static prefix reusable. Option A: the minimum cacheable length depends on the model and is at most 4,096 tokens, which 7,900 tokens already exceeds. Option C moves the breakpoint to the least stable content. Option D: cached content persists for minutes, not sub-second.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output)

References:
• Prompt caching — Best practices for effective caching
• Prompt caching — Cache limitations
• Prompt caching for Claude models — Use prompt caching (Google Cloud docs)

column2:
Your retail analytics app runs Claude Haiku 4.5 on Vertex AI and generates JSON pricing rules that users copy with one click. The user prompt already says 'Respond with only the JSON', yet 15% of responses still arrive wrapped in a markdown code fence with a sentence of explanation before or after it, which breaks the copy button.

Which of these changes most reliably returns only the JSON?

A. Add a second, stronger instruction in the system prompt forbidding any commentary or markdown fences.
B. Remove the markdown fence lines from each response with a regular expression before the result is shown to the user.
C. Lower temperature to 0 so that the model stops adding its explanations and code fences around the JSON output.
D. Prefill the assistant turn with an opening fence tagged json and set the closing fence as a stop sequence.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: prefilling makes Claude treat the opening fence as text it already wrote, so it proceeds straight into the JSON, and the closing-fence stop sequence ends generation before any trailing commentary; the stop sequence itself is not included in the output, leaving raw JSON. Option A is more of the prompt-only instruction that already fails 15% of the time. Option B removes the fence lines but leaves the sentence of explanation in the copied text, so the copy button still breaks. Option C affects randomness, not the habit of explaining. Currency note (Oct 2026): prefill is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, where a prefilled request returns a 400 error; for JSON output current docs point to structured outputs, and the exam guide to tool use with a JSON schema.

References:
• Prompting best practices — Migrating away from prefilled responses
• Request predictions with Claude models — Use a curl command (Google Cloud docs)
• Structured outputs — Why use structured outputs

column2:
Your media pipeline runs Claude Haiku 4.5 on Vertex AI, prefills the assistant turn with the opening of a fenced code block and sets the closing fence as a stop sequence. The post-processor then searches the response for the closing fence to cut the block out and raises an error on 100% of responses.

What explains this?

A. The stop sequence text is not included in the returned response; treat the block as ending where the response ends.
B. Stop sequences are ignored when a prefill is present; remove the prefill so that the fence is emitted.
C. The closing fence is returned with a trailing newline that the search does not match; trim the whitespace first.
D. The model emits the closing fence only when max_tokens is large enough; raise the limit.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: when Claude generates a stop sequence, generation halts and the matched text is excluded from the returned content, so the closing fence never appears and the response simply ends at the end of the block. Option B: prefill and stop sequences are designed to be combined. Option C: nothing at or after the stop sequence is returned at all. Option D: max_tokens has no bearing on stop-sequence exclusion. Currency note (Oct 2026): prefill is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, where a prefilled request returns a 400 error; stop sequences remain part of the Messages API.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Stop reasons and fallback — stop_sequence
• Create a Message (Claude API reference)
• Prompting best practices — Migrating away from prefilled responses

column2:
A logistics report service runs Claude Haiku 4.5 on Vertex AI and prefills the assistant turn with {"shipment_id": to force JSON output, then calls json.loads on message.content[0].text. Every call fails with a parse error at position 0, although the printed text looks like the rest of a valid object.

What is the fix?

A. Move the prefill into the user message as an instruction to repeat it verbatim at the start of the answer.
B. Set a stop sequence of } and add the closing brace back to the returned text before parsing.
C. Prepend the prefilled text to the returned text and parse the combined string with json.loads.
D. Raise max_tokens to give the model room to write the whole object, opening brace included.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Claude treats the prefilled content as text it has already written and continues from its end, and the API returns only the newly generated continuation, so you must stitch the prefill and the response together to reconstruct the full object. Option A turns steering text into an instruction with no guarantee. Option B cuts the text at the first closing brace and restores that brace, but the prefilled opening is still missing from the text being parsed, so the error at position 0 remains. Option D: nothing was truncated. Currency note (Oct 2026): prefill is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, where a prefilled request returns a 400 error; current docs use structured outputs to guarantee a JSON shape.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Request predictions with Claude models — Use a curl command (Google Cloud docs)
• Prompting best practices — Migrating away from prefilled responses
• Structured outputs — Why use structured outputs

column2:
Your media company's debate-prep tool runs Claude Haiku 4.5 on Vertex AI and must argue the assigned side of a motion. The system prompt states the side to defend, yet in 20% of runs Claude opens with 'There are strong arguments on both sides' and gives a balanced summary.

Which of these changes most directly commits the response to the assigned side?

A. Repeat the assigned side three times in the system prompt and add 'Do not be balanced' in capital letters at the end.
B. Generate two responses for every motion and keep the one whose first sentence does not mention both sides.
C. Set temperature to 0 so that the model stops varying its stance from one run of the tool to the next.
D. Prefill the assistant turn with 'The case for the motion is stronger because' so Claude continues that stance.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: prefilling puts words in Claude's mouth. It treats the prefilled assistant text as its own and continues consistently with it. Option A is more prompt-only pressure of the kind that already fails one run in five. Option B doubles cost and still yields balanced output when both runs hedge. Option C makes outputs repeatable, not committed; a hedging response at temperature 0 hedges every time. Currency note (Oct 2026): prefill is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, where a prefilled request returns a 400 error; current docs replace it with direct instructions in the prompt.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Prompting best practices — Migrating away from prefilled responses
• Request predictions with Claude models — Use a curl command (Google Cloud docs)
• Prompting best practices — Give Claude a role

column2:
A logistics operations report generator on Vertex AI asks Claude for a summary followed by an 'Appendix' section. Product wants only the summary in the customer email, but the prompt instruction 'omit the appendix' is ignored in 10% of responses, and cutting the summary with max_tokens truncates it mid-sentence.

Which change reliably ends the response before the appendix?

A. Lower max_tokens further and accept occasional truncation of the summary.
B. Set stop_sequences to the appendix heading so that generation halts as soon as it begins.
C. Add few-shot examples of summaries without appendices to the prompt.
D. Post-process the full response in code and delete everything after the appendix heading.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: stop sequences end generation the moment the specified string is produced, so the response contains the complete summary and nothing from the appendix, with the heading itself excluded; this controls length and format by content rather than by a token count. Option A trades one defect for another. Option C is still probabilistic guidance. Option D produces the right text but only after paying the tokens and latency for the appendix.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Stop reasons and fallback — stop_sequence
• Create a Message (Claude API reference)

column2:
Your logistics team runs a routing workflow on Vertex AI in which a classification call assigns each request to one of seven categories. The router prompt lists the categories by name alone, and each category has a pipeline with a specialized prompt and tool set. In the last month, 9% of requests concerned customs paperwork, and most of them mentioned a held shipment. A 'customs' category exists and its pipeline has the tools for that work, yet the router sent two thirds of those requests to 'tracking', whose pipeline lacks them, and users received irrelevant answers.

What is the right change?

A. Add a 'customs paperwork' category to the router and build a second pipeline with a prompt and tools for it.
B. Give the 'tracking' pipeline the customs tools and extend its prompt to cover requests about customs paperwork.
C. Describe each category in the router prompt, with example requests and how customs differs from tracking.
D. Have the router return its two closest categories and run both of their pipelines, keeping the better answer.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. A router chooses well only among categories it can tell apart, and this prompt gives it seven bare names while most customs requests mention a held shipment, which reads like tracking. The 'customs' pipeline and its tools already exist, so the misrouting comes from how the choice is described; stating each category's scope, typical requests and the boundary between customs and tracking addresses that cause directly and at low cost. Option A treats the problem as a missing route: a second customs category would overlap the existing one and make the choice harder. Option B stretches 'tracking' beyond its purpose, erodes the separation that keeps each pipeline reliable, and leaves the working customs pipeline unused. Option D doubles cost and latency on every request to work around a classification problem.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.2

References:
• Ticket routing — Define user intent categories
• Building effective agents — Workflow: Routing (Anthropic engineering)

column2:
Your retail analytics team scores product listings with a parallelization workflow on Vertex AI: six focused calls (title, images, pricing, compliance, description, shipping) run at once, and an aggregator call combines their six outputs into a final score. After a round of prompt edits, the final score's agreement with human reviewers fell from 94% to 81%. The team re-ran each of the six dimension prompts against its own labeled cases, and every dimension scored within one point of its result from before the edits.

What is the most efficient way to diagnose and fix the regression?

A. Evaluate the compliance prompt alone against a larger set of its labeled cases and iterate on just that prompt.
B. Merge the six dimension prompts and the aggregator into a single call and test that one prompt after each edit.
C. Move the six dimension calls to a larger model and re-run the full workflow against the reviewer scores.
D. Replay stored dimension outputs through the aggregator alone and iterate on its prompt against reviewer scores.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Each call in a parallelization workflow is a separate step that can be tested on its own, so a regression is traced by finding the step whose behavior changed. All six dimension prompts score as they did before the edits while the final score moved, so the fault lies in the aggregation step. Feeding the aggregator stored dimension outputs holds its inputs fixed, shows its behavior directly, and lets the team iterate on one prompt at the cost of one call per case. Option A re-tests a dimension that the team has already shown to be unchanged. Option B gives up the focused prompts and the per-step testability that made this diagnosis possible. Option C spends more on six healthy calls and leaves the aggregator as it is.

Your logistics team checks each shipment exception with a sequential chain of five focused Claude calls on Vertex AI, averaging 2 seconds each. The first call classifies the exception from the carrier scan. Each of the other four calls (customs, address, damage and billing checks) takes that classification as an input, and none of the four reads another's output. The operations lead asks how far converting the chain into a parallel fan-out, with an aggregator call of about 2 seconds, would cut the 10-second response time.

What should you tell the operations lead?

A. It falls to about 6 seconds, because the four checks run together after the classification call finishes.
B. It falls to about 4 seconds, because the five calls start together and the aggregator runs after them.
C. It stays near 10 seconds, because one dependency in a chain forces the five calls to keep their order.
D. It rises to about 12 seconds, because the aggregator is added while the five calls keep running in order.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Steps can run in parallel when none of them needs another's output, and a step that feeds others has to finish first. The classification call feeds all four checks, and the four checks are independent of one another, so the fastest valid shape is the classifier, then the four checks at once, then the aggregator: roughly 2 + 2 + 2 seconds. Option B assumes that all five calls are independent, which would suit a pure fan-out but ignores that four of them wait for the classification. Option C treats one dependency as binding every step, although only the first call has to precede the others. Option D keeps the whole chain sequential and adds the aggregator, overlooking the four independent checks.

Your logistics operations team handles its three most common request types on Vertex AI (reschedule delivery, update address, delivery exception) with fixed workflows, each running a set sequence of three tool calls. The first two workflows complete 99% of their requests. The 'delivery exception' workflow completes 61%. Log analysis shows that the lookup an exception needs at each step depends on what the previous lookup returned, so that a customs hold, a damage flag and a failed address check each lead somewhere different, and that the failed exceptions, which staff resolved by hand, needed 40 different lookup sequences last month.

What change most improves reliability?

A. Build 40 fixed workflows for 'delivery exception', one per observed lookup sequence, and add a router call that selects among them.
B. Hand 'delivery exception' requests to an agent that picks each tool call from the previous result, and keep the other two workflows.
C. Extend the 'delivery exception' workflow to run the full set of available lookups in a set order on each request it gets.
D. Replace the three workflows with a single agent that plans its own tool calls for each of the three request types.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. A fixed sequence suits work whose steps are known in advance; when each step depends on what the previous one found, the plan has to adapt as results arrive. Two request types complete 99% of the time on their fixed workflows, while the lookup a delivery exception needs at each step depends on what the previous lookup returned, which is why 40 different sequences appeared. Giving that one type to an agent that decides each call from the latest result fits the work, and the predictable types stay on the workflows that serve them well. Option A hard-codes sequences that branch on results a router cannot see when the request arrives, and new sequences will keep appearing. Option C runs lookups that do not apply and keeps a fixed order. Option D gives up the reliability of the two workflows that work.

A logistics team uses Claude from a Cloud Run job to convert 40-line YAML routing configurations to a new schema. The conversion renames the keys and regroups the entries, so almost no line of a file stays as it was. The current design gives Claude the text editor tool, and Claude issues about 35 str_replace commands per file, each in its own request and response. A file takes about 90 seconds, and 8% of files are left half-converted after a replacement fails to match the text it expects.

Which approach best fits this task?

A. Have Claude read each file once and write the complete converted file back in a single operation.
B. Keep the line-by-line replacements and have Claude quote three lines of context around each one.
C. Keep the line-by-line replacements and have Claude list them in a plan before it issues the first.
D. Split each file into four 10-line pieces and have Claude replace lines in one piece per request.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Targeted replacement suits a small change inside a large file, where output scales with the edit and untouched lines are left alone; a full read and write suits a change that touches the whole file. These files are 40 lines long and the conversion alters almost every line, so about 35 replacements cost 35 round trips, and each old_str has to match exactly a file that earlier replacements keep changing. One whole-file write outputs the new lines once, in a single step, with nothing to match. Option B makes each match more specific but keeps the 35 round trips, and the quoted context lines are themselves being rewritten. Option C adds planning without removing the round trips or the matching. Option D multiplies requests and keeps line-level edits.

A hospital billing team runs a nightly agent, built with the Claude Agent SDK, that updates one reimbursement rate in a 900-line fee schedule file. The agent has the built-in Read, Edit and Write tools, and its instructions tell it to read the file and write back the full updated contents. Each run spends about 12,000 output tokens, and in 6% of commits reviewers find other lines altered as well, such as a dropped comment or a reformatted block. Each rate sits on its own line beside a procedure code that appears once in the file.

Which change best addresses both the stray alterations and the token cost?

A. Have the agent call Edit with the procedure code as old_string and the updated rate as new_string.
B. Keep Read and Write, and move the agent to a larger model that reproduces long files more faithfully.
C. Have the agent call Edit with the rate's current line as old_string and the updated line as new_string.
D. Split the fee schedule into nine 100-line files and have the agent Read and Write the one holding the rate.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Write replaces a file with the full content supplied, so changing one rate that way means regenerating all 900 lines, and any line reproduced imperfectly lands in the commit. Edit performs an exact string replacement and requires old_string to appear exactly once; the rate's line carries a procedure code that occurs once in the file, so it is a valid anchor, the output is a single line, and the other lines are never regenerated. Option A misuses the same tool: Edit replaces old_string with new_string, so naming the procedure code as the text to replace would overwrite the code with the new rate and leave the old rate where it was. Option B raises cost and relies on a rewrite being exact, which a larger model does not ensure. Option D restructures a file to suit the tool and regenerates 100 lines on each run.

Your media company's research assistant on Vertex AI answers questions from sets of 40-page PDF reports. The pipeline sends each PDF as a document block with citations enabled, so each claim in an answer links to the page it came from. Editors complain that a figure on which three reports agree and a figure that one report calls a preliminary estimate from a small sample read the same way in an answer: both appear as flat statements, each with a valid page link.

What change best addresses the editors' complaint?

A. Require a page citation on each sentence of an answer and have the pipeline reject answers that contain an uncited sentence.
B. Have the assistant rate its confidence in each claim from 0 to 1 and leave out the claims that it scores below 0.8.
C. Have the assistant report the figures that appear in two or more reports and leave the single-report figures out of the answer.
D. Have the assistant keep each source's own qualifiers and set well-established findings apart from preliminary or contested ones.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. A page link shows where a claim came from; it does not show how well established the claim is. The citations in this pipeline already work, and what the answers lose is each report's own characterization of its finding, such as a preliminary estimate from a small sample, together with the fact that three reports agree on another figure. Carrying those qualifiers through and presenting well-established findings apart from preliminary or contested ones gives editors that distinction. Option A tightens location, which is not what is missing. Option B substitutes the model's self-rated confidence, an unreliable signal, for the sources' own wording, and hides claims that editors need to see. Option C discards single-report findings outright, although a clearly labeled preliminary figure is useful to an editor.

A media company's video agent on Vertex AI generates short clips with a bash tool that runs FFmpeg on a Compute Engine worker. After each render, the agent inspects the clip with the same tool, pulling frames and a timestamped caption transcript into the conversation to check that narration starts where the script calls for. In sessions of up to 20 clips, the check catches the timing defects. In sessions of 60 clips, from about the 35th clip onward the agent approves clips whose transcripts it never pulled and misreports offsets it measured for earlier clips.

Which change best keeps the check reliable across a 60-clip session?

A. Instruct the agent to pull twice as many frames and the full transcript for each clip before it approves the clip.
B. Have the agent delegate each clip's render and inspection to a subagent that returns a short verdict and offset.
C. Add a system prompt rule that the agent pulls the transcript for each clip before it approves that clip.
D. Move the agent to a model with a larger context window and keep each clip's frames and transcript in the conversation.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The check works early in a session and fails late, which points to the conversation filling with verbose inspection output, the frames and transcripts of dozens of clips, until the agent loses track of what it has measured. A subagent works in its own context and returns its final message alone, so each clip's frames and transcript stay out of the main conversation, which holds a short verdict per clip and stays focused on coordinating the batch. Option A adds more output per clip and brings the degradation on sooner. Option C restates a step the agent already follows while its context is small, and leaves the accumulation in place. Option D leaves it in place as well: a larger window holds more, but accuracy and recall degrade as the token count grows, and each request costs more.
